abstract:
This article assesses the impact of digital television on cognitive de-
velopment and educational inequality, and studies whether it depends on
the educational value of the alternative activities that digital television
crowds out.
I use heterogeneity in the timing of the television digital
switchover in the diﬀerent postcode areas in England to test for the previ-
ous. I ﬁnd that the digital switchover increased average grades of children
by 0.028 standard deviations, contributing to the human capital forma-
tion, and that this eﬀect was larger in schools at the bottom of the scores
distribution, reducing educational inequality. I also ﬁnd that the digital
switchover decreased the probability of children taking part in harmful
activities, and their frequency.

Introduction
Since its introduction in 1936, television has been one of the daily habits
for most individuals. On average, a person spends more than three hours and
a half per day watching TV (Ofcom, 2015). Concerns about its impact on the
behaviour emerged rapidly and have been feeded by evidence showing deleteri-
ous eﬀects of television viewing on inactivity, aggression, and sleep patterns of
children, who are arguably the most sensitive group of the population to televi-
sions inﬂuence (Zimmerman, 2005). Cognitive development is not an exception,
and it is widely believed by paediatricians that television viewing has a negative
impact on school achievement (Gentile et al. 2004).
During the last decade, there has been a positive trend on the average
scores of students in standarised exams in England. One example is the Key
Stage 2 (KS2) test, an external assessed exam taken by students by the later
stage of primary education, of which average grade has increased by 0.78 points.
At the same time, it has taken place the introduction of digital television, which
has been the ﬁrst signiﬁcant revolution in television technology since colour
television happened in the 1950s, and has introduced important adjustments
in the television market such as an increase in the number of channels from 5
to 40, an improvement in the television deﬁnition, additional services related
1
to multimedia, the possibility of watching television in diﬀerent languages, and
multiplexing, which is the ability of having more than one program in the same
channel.
In this paper, I identify whether the digitalization of the television indus-
try had an impact on educational inequality and on the cognitive development of
children, measured by their performance at the KS2 test. I also assess whether
television exposure impact on education depends critically on the educational
value of the alternative activities that it crowds out (Gentkow and Shapiro,
2008), by testing whether digitalization of television changed the extent in which
students are involved in harmful activities. Estimating the eﬀect on scores and
habits introduces identiﬁcation problems, as households could self-select into
the demand of digital television. To confront potential endogeneity problems,
I use a natural experiment consisting on the digital television switchover that
took place in UK. Between the end of 2008 and 2012, UK progressively adapted
by stages all its TV transmitters, most of which had been built in the 1960s
and 1970s, to stop broadcasting analogue TV but strengthen the power of the
digital TV signal. At the day when the switchover took place in a transmitter,
thousands of individuals obtained access for the ﬁrst time to an increase in the
supply of channels from 5 to 40. The decentralized location of the television
transmitters induced substantial geographical variation in the time when the
digital switchover occurred across the UK, with neighbouring postcode areas
obtaining accessibility to digital television at diﬀerent years, which created id-
iosyncratic diﬀerences in the receipt of free digital channels. This allows me
to use a diﬀerences-in-diﬀerences approach that compares test scores (habits)
across schools (children) and years, attending to the treatment status of each
observation. During the switchover process, 10 million of viewers were brought
availability of digital signal for the ﬁrst time, the daily amount of time dedi-
cated to watch television by an average person increased by 23 minutes per day
(Ofcom, 2015), and the share of audience of the main ﬁve channels decreased
by 12% (BARB, 2015).
To conduct the analysis, I use three main datasets. The ﬁrst was provided
by the Department of Education of UK on the aggregated results of pupils at
the school level in the KS2 test. The data includes test performance measures of
approximately 16,000 schools followed every year since 1991. My second dataset
comes from the youth questionnaire in the Understanding Society Survey, where
children respond questions about their lives, habits, or social activities they take
part in. This allows me to test the hypothesis of whether television exposure im-
pact on education depends critically on the educational value of the alternative
activities that it crowds out. Finally, I obtain my third dataset by webscraping
data, on the DigitalUK webpage, of the date when the digital switchover took
place at each postcode in England. After having assembled my third dataset, I
match it with the two former ones.
A key ﬁnding is that the digital switchover increased the average KS2 test
scores by 0.028 standard deviations. The impact was higher in schools with a
higher proportion of students who were economically disadvantaged or who had
other language than English as a ﬁrst language. Importantly, the magnitude of
2
the impact depends on the academic performance previous to the switchover,
with a stronger eﬀect on schools below the median, and no impact on schools
above it. This points that the digital switchover reduced educational inequality,
which suggests that television exposure impact on education depends critically
on the educational value of the alternative activities that it crowds out (Gentkow
and Shapiro, 2008). I ﬁnd evidence supporting this hypothesis. My preferred
estimates indicate that digital switchover reduced the probability of a kid having
ever drunk alcohol by 7.31 percentage points, and also decreased the frequency
in which kids consume alcohol. There are two possible mechanisms driving the
results in scores and habits: either digital television changed the time allocation
of low performance students, who substituted TV watching time for detrimen-
tal activities, or it increased the educational value of TV contents. I name the
former as the quantity mechanism, and the latter as the quality mechanism. I
ﬁnd that the digital switchover increased happiness in school and motivation to
get further education, but did not alter time allocation.
The present analysis is related to empirical studies that study the impact
of television on the cognitive skills development and reading habits formation
(Beentjes et al. (1988); Walberg & Tsai (1985); Rice (1987)). Whereas most
of the literature used to highlight a negative relationship between TV and cog-
nitive development (Christakis et al. (2004); Timmer et al. (1985); Hancox
et al.
(2005)), recent research has shed light on a potential positive impact
(Gentkow & Shapiro (2008)). This paper is also related to empirical papers on
the importance of TV contents on behavior and academic skills accumulation
(Wright et al. (2001)). There is evidence of academic achievement being lowered
when exposed to pure entertainment and violent content (Kirkorian, Wartella,
and R. Anderson, 2008), adult aggression increasing due to TV-violence view-
ing (Huesmann, Moise-Titus, Podolski and D. Eron, 2003) and harmful habits
becoming more frequent because of TV watching (Robinson, L. Chen and D.
Killen, 1998), but also there is evidence of cognitive and academic enhancement
as a response of exposure to age appropriate programs designed around an ed-
ucational curriculum (Bryant et al. (2004); Fisch (2004); Calvert (2003)). This
ambiguous evidence may be explained by TV programs displacing diﬀerently
non-TV activities depending on their content (C. Huston et al (1999)). From a
policy perspective, if TV contents alter cognitive development, deregulation of
content availability may bring a considerable eﬀect on educational attainment.
Last but not least, my paper relates to the empirical literature on the impor-
tance of the TV industry on social attitudes, perceptions and behaviour (Jensen
and Oster (2009); La Ferrara (2007); Mastrorocco and Minale (2015); Gentkow
(2006); DellaVigna and Kaplan (2007)).
This paper contributes to the previous literature in that (i) I examine the
access to digital television, which caused a change both in the time that people
view TV and in the contents they watch, instead of television, (ii) I use a large
panel dataset based on external assessed examinations to study the impact on
cognitive development, instead of using survey or school self-reported data (iii)
I use a diﬀerence in diﬀerence approach at the ﬁner geographical level of the
postcode area, and (iv) I use an additional panel dataset based on the youth
3
questionnaire of the Understanding Society Survey, to test whether the impact
on test scores comes from a change in habits, and to study the mechanism that
drives the results in scores and habits.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II describes
digital TV industry and its introduction. Section III presents the data. Sec-
tion IV contains the empirical strategy and results on education. In Section V
presents estimates of the eﬀect of digital television on habits, and of the mech-
anism that drives the results. Section VII concludes.
2
Digital Television
Digital television has been the ﬁrst signiﬁcant revolution in television
technology after colour television happened in the 1950s. It has several advan-
tages over its analogue predecessor, such as the provision of more digital channels
in the same space, higher deﬁnition, additional services related to multimedia,
the possibility of watching TV in diﬀerent languages, and multiplexing, which is
the ability of having more than one program in the same channel. However, the
most important feature of digital television is the increase from the 5 channels
that could be watched through the analogue aerial to the 40 diﬀerent channels
that can currently be watched through the digital signal.
In 2004, The British Government delegated Ofcom.1 and Digital UK.2
jointly the task of discontinuing analogue television broadcasting on a transmit-
ter group.3 basis. Meanwhile Ofcom amended the broadcast licences requiring
the delivery of the analogue switch-oﬀaccording to a speciﬁc timetable, Digital
UK organised the programme of the digital switchover, managed the upgrade
of the television transmitters, and ensured that individuals were supported and
understood the process. The digital switchover, or cessation of the analogue
television transmission, was done in stages, from the end of 2008 to 2012, where
transmitter groups ceased broadcasting analogue television services at diﬀer-
ent deadlines to start transmitting high-power digital signal. The switchover
process is approximately represented in Figure 1. More accurate details of the
switchover timetable can be found in Table A.1 of Appendix.
1Ofcom is the communications regulator in the UK
2Digital UK is the independent, not-for-proﬁt organisation, funded by the public-service
broadcasters and multiplex operators
3A transmitter group is a bunch of transmitters, one principal transmitter and several
relay transmitters, each of which provides TV signal.
The former broadcast TV signal to
individuals and to a number of the later type of transmitters, which repeat the TV signal to
many other individuals who could not receive TV signal from former.
4
[H]
Figure 1: Stages of the Digital Switchover in England
Digital signal in the television market in UK is provided by 1150 sepa-
rate transmitters serving to 26 million of homes. There are 81 main transmitters
located across diﬀerent parts of the UK, and 1,154 relay transmitter sites, which
receive TV signal from the former and repeat it to those households living far
from the main transmitters. Before switchover, one-in-four households could
not receive digital television via an aerial. This was independent of whether
these households had already adapted their television set in order to be able
to receive digital TV. The reason is that, TV transmitters were broadcasting
digital and analogue signal at the same time, which decreases the strength of the
coverage of the prior signal. As a consequence, digital signal could only reach
households who were both located close to a TV transmitter and not aﬀected
by adverse geographical factors. At the time when the switchover happened
in a transmitter group, it ceased broadcasting analogue television services and
started transmitting high-power digital signal, making digital signal available
for the latter group of households.
Importantly, each postcode area in England receives TV signal from sev-
eral and diﬀerent TV transmitters, each of which may have diﬀerent digital
switchover dates. This is the reason why I deﬁne the date when the digital
switchover occurred in a particular postcode area as the earliest date among
the switchover dates of the TV transmitters providing signal to that postcode.
The switchover process made digital TV through an aerial (Freeview) available
to all homes, with 10 million of viewers been brought into Freeview coverage
for the ﬁrst time. Additionally, there were millions of households who could
receive digital signal through an aerial before the switchover, but who had not
still adapted their TV sets to receive it. In fact, only three years before the
switchover started, more than three-quarters of homes were still analogue on at
least one TV (Ofcom 2012). As a consequence, there were additional millions
of short-sighted individuals who were able to watch digital TV only weeks or
days before the switchover happened.
Digital switchover may have had an impact on the cognitive development
of children through a quantity or a quality mechanism. The former means that
the higher variety in the TV programs induced children stop doing alternative
activities to watch more TV. The latter means that the increase in the number
of channels brought a change in the TV contents watched by children, and so
5
in the intrinsic values that children obtain from watching TV.
Figure 2: Quantity channel
The quantity mechanism came in the form of an increase in the time dedi-
cated to watch TV by children, from 134 minutes per day before switchover to
142 by the end of it (Ofcom, 2015). After 2012, year in which the switchover
ﬁnished, there has been a continuous decrease in the average time of TV watch-
ing in UK. Possible explanations are the growing popularity in take-up of non-
broadcast, on-demand services such as Netﬂix and Amazon Prime Instant Video,
as well as the growth in connectivity and mainstream adoption of smartphones
and tablets that have taken place since 2012, and that are likely to have reduced
traditional and broadcast TV-set viewing (Ofcom, 2015). Figure 2 represents
the quantity mechanism.
The quality mechanism came from a drastic decrease in the audience
share of the main ﬁve channels after the switchover , from 63.5% in 2007 to
51% in 2013, in favour of the newly available digital channels (Ofcom, 2015).
The new channels have diﬀerent TV contents than the main channels, and so
transmit diﬀerent intrinsic values, which could have aﬀected behaviour and cog-
nitive development of children. Digital television also allowed viewers with the
possibility of watching TV in diﬀerent languages, which may have stimulated
the verbal abilities of kids. Figure 3 represents the quality mechanism.

Data
3.1
Schooling Data
I obtained my data on academic performance from the Department of
Education of UK. This dataset contains academic information of students in
the KS2 exam, aggregated at the school level. In particular, the dataset is a
panel that includes KS2 test performance measures of 16,000 schools in Eng-
land, followed every year during the period 1991-2016. KS2 test is an external
assessed exam taken by eleven years old students by their later stage of pri-
mary education in the month of May, and consist of sections on mathematics;
English grammar; punctuation and spelling, and writing. KS2 test is graded in
a scale of 0 to 33 points, even though most of the schools are centered around
the national average point score, which is 27. Figure 4 represents the average
grade distribution of schools during the diﬀerent years that I use in the analysis.
A mapping of point scores to levels can be found in the Appendix A of the paper.
7
[H]
Figure 4: Yearly average grades distribution
There have been two important reforms in the structure of KS2 ex-
ams. Firstly, this test was based in an English, Maths and Science part until
2009. However, the latter ended in 2009, and Average Points Score were recal-
culated by the Department of Education back to 2007 on the basis of English
and Maths test results, making 2007-2009 comparable with later years. Because
of the change in the exam format, I only include the years after 2006 in the anal-
ysis. Secondly, before 2012, the maximum grade that could be obtained in the
KS2 exam was 35, but from 2012 onwards, the highest score attainable increased
to 39. In addition, since 2012, the results in the writing part of the KS2 exams
have been based on the teacher assessment of the work that students have made
during the last year of primary education, instead of being externally assessed.
During the analysis, I use time ﬁxed eﬀects and school individual trends to con-
trol for these changes.
The dataset has information on several academic performance indicators
for each school, such as the average test score, or the percentage of students with
a level of 4 or higher in the Maths and English section, or in the overall test,
among others. The ’Key Stage 2 average point score’ is a much more granular
measure of attainment than the ’Percentage of pupils achieving the national ex-
pected level or higher’, because it shows how far are students performing with
respect to the national expected level. In addition to these academic perfor-
mance measures, there is information on school characteristics such as the total
number of students, or the percentage of students with a language other than
English as the ﬁrst language, among others.
The schools in the dataset are state-funded schools. I exclude Community
Special Schools and Foundation Special Schools from the analysis since these
type of schools have only been operating since 2010. In addition, as indepen-
dent schools are not required to enter their pupils for the tests, the Department
8
of Education does not publish KS2 results data for them. Neither there is in-
formation of schools with cohorts of fewer than 6 pupils, as the Department
of Education does not publish their results due to its privacy policy. Within
schools, every student in year 6 of primary education is eligible to take the key
stage 2 test. An eligible student may still not take the test if they have not yet
reached the level of ability required to sit these tests, or if a disability prevents
them from being able to access the tests. However, the Department of Educa-
tion includes every child registered for tests in their calculation of performance
measures, regardless of whether they actually sit the test, and only accepts a
school’s request to remove a child from the calculations if the student has a
limited English and has arrived from a non-English speaking country within the
last two years.
3.2
Digital television data
I obtained my data on the date when the digital switchover took place at
the postcode area level by webscraping the DigitalUK organisations webpage,
which provides information about which TV transmitters that provide signal to
a speciﬁc postcode area, and about the quality of the signal. More generally, this
dataset contains information on the year when the digital switchover took place
on each of the postcodes contained in my schooling dataset. The importance
of having postcode level data lies in the fact that each postcode area receives
TV signal from several TV transmitters, which may have had diﬀerent digital
switchover dates. As a result, I deﬁne the date of the digital switchover in a par-
ticular postcode area as the earliest date among the switchover dates of the TV
transmitters providing signal to that postcode. Figure 7 draws a hypothetical
postcode area receiving digital signal from diﬀerent TV transmitters, located
at diﬀerent TV regions.
These are: the main transmitters A, B, C, E, and
the relay transmitter that receives signal from main transmitter D. Assuming
that the main transmitters A-E have diﬀerent digital switchover dates, which is
the same than the date of their respective relay transmitters, then the digital
switchover date for the green postcode area is the earliest among the switchover
dates of transmitters A-E.
9
[H]
Figure 5: Explanation of digital switchover
The implicit assumption I make to match my educational and digital
TV datasets is that students live in the postcode area of the school they attend,
and so, students of a school are aﬀected by the digital switchover at the time
that it occurs in the postcode area of the school. This is consistent for two
main reasons. Firstly, most of schools in UK receive more applications than
places available, and distance from the permanent home address of the child
to the school is one of the main factors taken into consideration when selecting
which students to admit. Secondly, I do not expect children to attend a school
far away from home, given the time costs that would be incurred. The match
between the Department of Education data and the digital TV data reduces the
initial sample of schools to 160,776 observations.
3.3
Understanding Society survey data
My data on time use and leisure comes from the youth questionnaire of
the Understanding Society Survey, with geographical special license at the Lower
Layer Superoutput area (LSOA).4 unit. The Understanding Society survey is
a UK Household longitudinal survey of the members of approximately 40,000
households in the United Kingdom during the period that goes from 2009 to
2014. Households recruited at the ﬁrst round of data collection are visited each
4LSOAs are geographical units designed with a minimum population ﬁgure of 1000 and a
mean population ﬁgure of 1500 and each consists of a grouping of Output Areas, typically ﬁve
10
year to collect information on changes to their household and individual circum-
stances. As part of the Understanding Society, approximately 3,000 household
members aged from 10 to 15 years old are asked to complete a self-completion
youth questionnaire about their lives, experiences, habits, or the social activities
in which they get involved. In particular, the youth survey contains questions
on how happy they are with their school and own work; on the leisure activities
they are involved in, such as the frequency in which they watch television, use
computer, play with game console, go out during the night, smoke, or drink
alcohol, among others; and on demographic characteristics such as age, sex and
parents income. The analysis of the impact that the digital switchover has on
some of these leisure activities is important to test the hypothesis of whether
television exposure impact on education depends critically on the educational
value of the alternative activities that it crowds out.
The Understanding society survey contains an individual identiﬁer vari-
able unique to each sampled child answering to the youth questionnaire, which
allows me to use child ﬁxed eﬀects. I use the LSOA, which is the smallest ge-
ographical unit that I can observe in the survey, to include information about
the date when the switchover takes place in the postcode area where each indi-
vidual interviewed lives. There are 34,378 LSOAs in England and Wales, and
I randomly select a postcode within each of the LSOAs where the individuals
interviewed live.
This does not constitute a problem for the analysis, given
that the LSOA is a very precise geographical unit, so that when the switchover
happens in any of the postcodes of a particular LSOA, it is very likely that it
has occurred at the same time for the entire LSOA. I then use Java software to
webscrape information about the date when the digital switchover takes place
on each of the postcodes where individuals interviewed live, and combine this
information with the Understanding Society dataset using the postcode as a
merging unit, which reduces the initial sample of individuals to 15,069 observa-
tions.

Empirical Framework
4.1
Summary Statistics

schools in England, and their respective postcode areas, were aﬀected by it
at diﬀerent points in time. Figure 6 represents the percentage of schools that

students do the KS2 exam, of every year during the period 2007-2014. It is
important to study whether schools aﬀected at diﬀerent points in time by the
digital switchover were already diﬀerent in my variables of interest before the
process had even started. Column 1 of Table 1 presents unweighted summary
statistics on the 16,000 schools in my sample. In the year before the switchover
process started, the average grade of a school was 27.55 points, and 27.58 only

4.2
Possible selection problems
In this paper, I compare the academic performance of diﬀerent treatment
groups of schools that were aﬀected by the digital switchover at diﬀerent times
during the period 2008-2012. One possible threat to the analysis is that the
assignment of treatment is not random. For example, digital switchover could
have been implemented earlier in areas where there is a higher demand of TV
time viewing, which may be correlated with the academic performance of chil-
dren. Therefore, it is important to study the nature of the digital television
switchover, to check whether digital television expanded ﬁrst in regions that
were performing diﬀerently in KS2 tests than later adopters. If this is the case,
the eﬀect that the digital switchover has on grades would be only capturing
previous grading trends.
To face possible selection problems, I estimate whether previous grade
trends or demographic characteristics of schools predict the timing of the digi-
tal switchover. To state this approach more formally, let ys be a variable that
takes value 1 if the school s is a late adopter of digital television (if it is aﬀected
by the digital switchover in 2011 or after) and 0 if the school is an early adopter
13
(when it is aﬀected before 2011). Let ags,07 and ags,08 be the average grade of
school s in the years 2007 and 2008 respectively. Xs,07 and Xs,08 are a set of
controls that include the total number of students with special needs and the
total number of students in school s in 2007 and 2008 respectively. Therefore, I
estimate the following probability model:
ys = α + βags,07 + λags,08 + φXs,07 + γXs,08 + εs
(1)
Where εs is a school level error term. A ﬁrst speciﬁcation (column
1 of Table 2) addresses the concern of whether previous average grades have
any eﬀect on the date when the digital switchover takes place for the diﬀerent
postcode areas, ﬁnding that higher grades in the year before the start of the
switchover process decreases the probability of being a late adopter. After con-
trolling for demographic controls for the years before the switchover (column 2
of Table 2), I ﬁnd that the previous eﬀect becomes insigniﬁcant but that higher
grades two years before the switchover increases the probability of being a late
adopter. A late adoption of the digital switchover is also more likely in larger
schools: a one percent increase in the size of a school in 2008 is associated with
a 0.2 percentage point increase in the likelihood of a school being aﬀected by the
digital switchover in a late stage. Given that bigger schools tend to be in urban
areas, this result suggests that digital switchover was implemented at ﬁrst place
in a higher proportion of rural areas, leaving cities for the end of the process.
Schools with a higher number of students with special needs in 2007 and 2008
are also more likely to be late adopters.
In column 3, I add local educational authority ﬁxed eﬀects to control for
geographic heterogeneity in the digital switchover penetration, capturing the de-
terminants of within-local educational authority digital TV availability. Neither
previous average grade trends nor past values of schools demographic charac-
teristics have an impact on the implementation of the digital switchover in the
diﬀerent areas. In particular, previous grades seem to be negatively correlated
with the probability of a school being a late adopter, although insigniﬁcant.
In sum, I ﬁnd that previous grades trends are uncorrelated with the tim-
ing at which the digital switchover takes place in the diﬀerent postcode areas

4.5
Heterogeneity
My results have so far been centred on the eﬀect that the digital switchover
had on the average academic performance of schools. In many cases, however,
it is relevant to study how this eﬀect changes depending on the characteristics
of schools, especially when looking at the sociodemographic attributes of their
students.
Prior literature shows a positive relationship between background
socioeconomic status and school performance (Sirin (2005); White (1982)). Al-
ternatively, television has been studied to improve language academic perfor-
mance for the minorities that do not have English as a ﬁrst language (Gentkow
& Shapiro (2008)). If in-home learning is greater in households with more ad-
vantaged backgrounds or with higher educational resources, then, an increase in
the supply of TV channels, which makes television more appealing, may be more
beneﬁcial for disadvantaged students, since it will displace activities and habits
with diﬀerent educational value depending on the socioeconomic status of stu-
dents. Alternatively, it could happen that socioeconomic advantaged students
choose to watch relatively more educational value added TV programs than
disadvantaged students (Wright et al. (2001)). The introduction of new TV
contents may change the type of programmes that children watch, the intrinsic
values they obtain through watching TV, and also the way in which they behave
or the activities they do, depending on their socioeconomic status. In column
1 of Table 4, I estimate speciﬁcation (2) adding a term that is an interaction
between the dummy that accounts for the digital switchover introduction and a
dummy that takes value 1 if the school has more than 40% of students eligible
for free school meals or looked after (25% of the sample satisﬁes this condition),
and 0 otherwise . The estimated eﬀect of digital switchover on average test
scores is almost the triple for schools with a high proportion of students with
free school meals, so that the digital television actually beneﬁts more to stu-
dents who cannot dispose of large educational resources. The eﬀect disappears
for the disadvantaged group after a year with accessibility to digital television.
An additional year since the switchover is positive, albeit insigniﬁcant, for the
rest of the sample.
The next column compare schools depending on their total number of
students by controlling for an interaction between the dummy that accounts
for the digital switchover introduction and a dummy that takes value 1 if the
school is below the average total number of students (237) and 0 otherwise. The
eﬀect is four times higher in bigger schools, suggesting that rural areas were not
necessarily the more aﬀected ones by the digital switchover.
Columns 3 compares schools with a high and low proportion of students
with English as ﬁrst language. The estimated eﬀect for non-English students
is almost the triple than for native students, indicating that digital television
improves the language and verbal abilities of the minorities that are not En-
glish native speakers. Still, the eﬀect continues being positive and signiﬁcant
for the rest of the sample, suggesting that the improvement of language skills of
non-natives was not the only mechanism through which the digital switchover
improved the academic performance of students.

The following column test whether the digital switchover aﬀected dif-
ferently schools depending on their proportion of students with special needs.

needs that is higher than 5.5% (10% of the sample), with the rest of schools.
The estimates indicate that the eﬀect is negative for the group of schools with

critically on the educational value of the alternative activities that it crowds out
(Gentkow and Shapiro, 2008). The following sections corroborate whether the

done more frequently. The variables of having ever tried alcohol or smoked are
dummy variables, which take value 0 when the child has never done it, and
1 otherwise. Importantly, digital switchover reduces the frequency in which a
child aged from 10 to 15 drinks alcohol, and also reduces the probability of
having drunk at some point in life by 5.2 percentage points. The reductions in
the frequency of drinking and in the probability of having tried alcohol dilutes
over time, given that the coeﬃcient of an additional year of digital television
is positive, albeit insigniﬁcant in the case of the frequency of drinking. Digital
switchover also decreases the frequency of smoking, the probability of having
smoked, and the frequency in which the child arrives late home, albeit these
estimates are insigniﬁcant. The eﬀects also seem to dilute over time, except in
the case of the frequency in which the child smokes, which decreases even more
over time. These results suggest that the positive impact that the availability
to a higher number of channels had on the cognitive development of children
comes through a reduction in some harmful activities that children do in their
leisure time, as a response of the digital switchover.
The impact that the digital switchover had on the academic per-
formance and habits of children may have occurred via two diﬀerent mecha-
nisms, the quantity and the quality mechanism. The former lies in the digital
switchover having induced children to watch more TV instead of doing lower
educational value added activities, and the latter consists on new TV contents
having beneﬁted behaviour and habits through the intrinsic values that new TV
programmes transmit, and so improving motivation and cognitive development.

To test whether the quantity mechanism drove the increase in academic
performance and reduction in harmful habits, I use two categorical variables
that take values from 1 to 5, to respectively measure the time that child i dedi-
cates to watch television during the week days and weekend, and include them
as dependent variables in speciﬁcation (4). I ﬁnd that estimates do not follow
the same direction and are insigniﬁcant, with the exception of the positive im-
pact of an additional year of digital television availability on the TV watching
time during weekends. The improvement in grades and habits seems not to be
driven by the quantity mechanism.
To test for the quality mechanism, I implement my baseline speciﬁcation
(4), using as dependent variable the answer to several questions about intrinsic
values in the youth questionnaire, which are measured by categorical variables
that take a higher number for higher values of the intrinsic value which is being
measured. I group the variables that I use to measure the quality mechanism
in three main groups: (i) motivation to obtain more education, (ii) interest,
concentration and attention in school, and (iii) culture and concerns with so-
cial problems. New TV contents may have enhanced behaviour and habits by
increasing any of the previous groups of intrinsic values.
Estimates are presented in Table 7 and 8. As regard to motivation, I ﬁnd
that digital switchover has a positive and signiﬁcant impact on the happiness to-
wards school work and on the inclination to take tertiary education, suggesting
that it increased motivation of children towards education. Digital switchover
does not have a signiﬁcant impact on any other measure of motivation, but an
additional year since the switchover decreases the conﬁdence that children have
on themselves, contributing to the dilution of the eﬀect that digital switchover
has on grades and habits. On the side of attentional problems, I ﬁnd that dig-
ital switchover increases conﬁdence, decreases concentration problems and the
frequency in which a child misbehaves at school, albeit insigniﬁcant. I also ﬁnd
that it has a negative and insigniﬁcant impact in constancy. The balance of ac-
cessibility to a higher number of channels on attentional problems seems to be
positive, although insigniﬁcant. Finally, there is mixed evidence of the impact
that the digital switchover had on social concerns. While the digital switchover
increases the frequency in which children volunteer, it also leads children to
care less about the others, be less helpful, and less interested in politics. These
estimates are insigniﬁcant.
This suggests that the impact that digital television had on academic
performance and habits was generated by an increase in the motivation, and
so, through the quality mechanism. More generally, new TV contents increased
motivation of children to obtain education, which improved the way they be-
have. It is important to bear in mind three possible limitations. First of all,
the quantity and quality mechanisms are imperfectly measured by using a set
of questions as a proxy. Secondly, the answers to the questions in the Under-
standing Society survey are self-completed, so that the response to them may
be subjectively biased. Finally, some of the questions that measure my quantity
and quality channel are only present in some of the years in which the Under-
standing Society survey was carried out, which reduces the precision of some
27
of my estimates. The last limitation does not play a role in my measure of
happiness with school work however, given that this question is present in every
year in which the survey was carried out. In summary, even though the last
set of regressions suggests that the quality mechanism, and in particular moti-
vation, was the cause of the positive impact that the digital switchover had on
grades and harmful habits, I cannot disregard the possibility that the quantity
mechanism, or that the quality mechanism via an improvement in attention or
social concerns, may have also been the mechanism through which the cognitive
development and behaviour were improved.

Conclusions
This paper studies the eﬀect of digital television on cognitive develop-
ment and habits. For this purpose, I use the digital switchover that took place
from 2008 to 2012 in UK. This induces a natural experiment: the timing of
entry of the digital switchover by stages in the diﬀerent postcode areas. I ﬁrstly
estimate whether a sudden increase in the number of TV channels, as part of
the analogue switch-oﬀ, has an eﬀect on the academic performance of children
at their last stage of primary education. I then test whether the impact on
grades comes as a response of a change in the habits of children, and lately,
I study whether the eﬀect on grades and habits is caused by a quantity or a
quality mechanism.
I ﬁnd a signiﬁcand and positive eﬀect of the digital switchover on aca-
demic performance.
Schools in postcode areas where the digital switchover
has already occurred score 0.028 standard deviations higher on KS2 average
scores than schools that had still not been aﬀected by the analogue switch-
oﬀ, suggesting that digital switchover contributed to the academic development
and formation of human capital. The eﬀect was driven by educational institu-
tions performing at the bottom of the test scores distribution before the digital
switchover started, with the lowest quartile of schools improving the average
grade by 0.071 standard deviations, and with the top quartiles having no signif-
icant boost in marks, which suggests that digital switchover reduced the educa-
tional inequality in England. Importantly, the positive impact is a short-term
eﬀect, disappearing three years after digital switchover has been implemented.
I also ﬁnd that the analogue switch-oﬀreduces both the probability of doing
and the frequency in which students do some harmful habits. In particular, the
digital switchover decreases the probability of a child having ever drunk alco-
hol by 7.31 percentage points, and also the frequency in which children drink
alcohol. The accessibility to digital television also decreases other harmful ac-
tivities such as smoking or arriving late at home, albeit insigniﬁcant. These
results are consistent with the eﬀect that I ﬁnd on academic achievement, and
conﬁrm the hypothesis that television exposure impact on education depends
critically on the educational value of the alternative activities that it crowds out

time viewing displacing harmful activities, and so academic performance of the
more problematic children, or it increased intrinsic values such as motivation
or consciousness about the negative implications of having bad habits, which
enhanced habits and academic performance. I test for these two mechanisms
in the ﬁnal part of the paper, ﬁnding that the positive impact of the digital
switchover on grades and habits comes through the quality mechanism, where
motivation to study is increased as a response of the new TV contents. Despite
ﬁnding that the digital switchover increases motivation, I am not able to reject
the possibility that the quantity mechanism, and so a change in the time allo-
cation, was one of the reasons driving the enhancement in grades and habits.
This paper leaves a number of open questions on the impact of the digital
switchover. First, the paper makes use of a school level dataset to analyse the
eﬀect of digital TV accessibility on school achievement. While it is true that
the analysis could beneﬁt from using a student level dataset, it is also true that
KS2 tests are taken every year by a diﬀerent cohort of students, so that it would
not be possible to account for unobserved student ﬁxed eﬀects even if I used a
pupil level dataset on the KS2 performance. Another possibility is to compare
the diﬀerence in the performance between the KS2 and the KS4 evaluation,
which is the test that follows the KS2 exam, across students who have been
aﬀected and who have not by the digital switchover in the meantime between
both assessments. In ongoing research, I use the national pupil dataset in order
to study the eﬀect of the digital switchover using individual data. However,
it is important to bear in mind that, once students have taken the KS2 test,
they usually take ﬁve years to do KS4 tests, meaning that the analysis may be
subject to an important amount of unobserved heterogeneity that could have
occurred in the meantime between both examinations. Second, I measure my
quantity and quality mechanism using a set of self-completed questions about
emotions, habits, and intrinsic values as a proxy, which are imperfect measures
of both mechanisms and are subject to personal biases. Even though I am not
able to use alternative private data given budget constraints, the use of non-
public datasets that give more speciﬁc information about the TV time viewing
of children living in diﬀerent postcode areas in England, may help to test my
hypothesis of whether the impact on cognitive development and habits is be-
ing driven by the quantity or quality mechanism. Finally, I hope that more
evidence on the eﬀect of other sources of technology shocks, such as the intro-
duction of internet broadband connection, or the implementation of mobile data
and smartphones, will complement the evidence in this paper.
